The Blue-capped manakin Lepidothrix coronata lays eggs that are modest in size, with a mean length of 18.4 millimeters and a width of 13.4 millimeters; these dimensions yield an initial wet weight of 1.73 grams [Ww0 = 1.73 grams] for the freshly laid egg. Such an egg mass is quite typical for a passerine of its body size and reflects the relatively small investment per offspring characteristic of the Pipridae. Incubation under controlled laboratory conditions reveals that the age at birth, or hatching interval, is 15 days [ab = 15 days] when the eggs are maintained at a constant temperature of 32 °C [T = 32 °C]. This developmental period is somewhat abbreviated compared to that of larger manakin congeners, potentially as an adaptation to the high ambient temperatures and constant predation pressure of lowland rainforest environments. Hatchlings emerge altricial and entirely dependent on maternal provisioning during the initial nestling phase, a stage that imposes considerable energetic demands on the attending female who must balance brooding against frequent foraging trips to gather fruit and small arthropods for the developing chick.

Females of Lepidothrix coronata attain an ultimate wet weight of 8.5 grams [Wwi = 8.5 grams] at adulthood, while the more elaborately ornamented males reach a slightly lower adult body mass of 8.1 grams [Wwi = 8.1 grams]. This subtle sexual dimorphism in mass, with females being about five percent heavier than males, is likely linked to the energetic burdens of egg production and incubation, a pattern observed across many lek-breeding passerines. The maximum recorded longevity for this species has been documented at 2,920 days [am = 2,920 days] in wild individuals studied through capture-mark-recapture programs when ambient conditions approximate 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. Such a lifespan is relatively extended for a small frugivore and probably reflects the low extrinsic mortality rates associated with a diet rich in high-energy lipids found in understory fruits. The substantial gap between the female body mass and that of the male becomes particularly relevant during the breeding season, when gravid females must allocate considerable resources toward the development of a single, relatively large egg compared to their own body size.

Under the sustained metabolic conditions that characterize the active foraging period of this species at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], the fledging period proceeds rapidly: nestlings achieve their first flight and depart the nest at 15 days after hatching [tx = 15 days after hatching]. This abbreviated nestling phase is a common tactic among small passerines that nest in open cup structures vulnerable to snake and primate depredation, where minimizing the time spent in the nest dramatically reduces cumulative predation risk. Sexual maturation follows a substantially longer trajectory, with puberty occurring at 42 days after hatching [tp = 42 days after hatching] when assessed under the same thermal regime at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This delayed onset of gonadal activity relative to fledging allows young birds to refine their foraging skills, develop flight proficiency, and establish social networks within lekking arenas before attempting to breed. The interval between achieving sexual maturity and initiating reproductive activity is often shaped by social competition, as young males must compete vigorously with older, more experienced display partners for access to territorial perches and female attention.

First reproduction in Lepidothrix coronata is typically deferred until 365 days after hatching [tR = 365 days after hatching] when ambient temperatures reach 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], meaning that individuals do not breed during their first year of life despite having reached puberty many months earlier. This reproductive delay is common among lek-breeding species where males require extended periods to establish dominance hierarchies and perfect complex vocal and visual displays that are critical for mate attraction. Females also benefit from this protracted maturation interval, as they can accumulate sufficient body condition to support the high metabolic costs of egg formation and incubation without compromising their own survival probability. The maximum reproductive rate, expressed as nearly two clutches per year [F_R_i = nearly two clutches per year], indicates that individual females are capable of producing multiple broods within a single breeding season given favorable food availability and adequate nest success. Each clutch consists of exactly one or two eggs [N_R_i = Each clutch consists of exactly one or two eggs], and the ability to renest rapidly following predation or fledging success contributes substantially to the species' overall fecundity.

Metabolic rate measurements obtained through flow-through respirometry provide insight into the substantial energetic demands experienced by this species under thermal conditions characteristic of its lowland habitat. The maximum basal metabolic rate recorded for Lepidothrix coronata reaches 36.36 milliliters per hour [JOi = 36.36 milliliters per hour] when measured at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], a value that reflects the high thermoregulatory costs imposed by ambient temperatures near the upper critical limit of the species' thermoneutral zone. A second, somewhat lower estimate of the maximum BMR has been reported at 27 milliliters per hour [JOi = 27 milliliters per hour] under identical thermal conditions, likely reflecting individual variation in body condition, molt status, or substrate-specific metabolic responses at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. Such elevated oxygen consumption rates underscore the physiological challenges faced by small-bodied frugivores in warm, humid environments where evaporative cooling via panting and gular fluttering imposes additional water and energy penalties. In comparative perspective, the mass-specific metabolic rate of this manakin is elevated relative to that of temperate-zone passerines of comparable body size, presumably as an adaptive response to the consistently high ambient temperatures and abundant food resources that characterize Neotropical rainforest understories.
